passage:
Mentor's note, Friday. Rashmi here, writing up the five weeks I sat in on Joseph's team.
Tuesday after the first investor chat, Joseph told everyone to add an AI helper. Two weeks later, after another chat, the plan became fast delivery. Last week, after a third, it turned into a marketplace. Each time, half-built work was put aside.
At the Thursday stand-up one engineer said quietly, "We never finish a test before the next idea arrives." Nobody replied, and two people looked at their laptops.
I asked Joseph what the numbers said about any of the three. There were no numbers, because nothing ran long enough to measure. We agreed to talk again on Monday.

qa.q: Which three ideas did the product swing toward?
qa.a: It swung toward an AI helper, fast delivery and a marketplace.

qa.q: What does the engineer's remark at the stand-up suggest about how the team felt?
qa.a: It suggests the engineer felt frustrated and doubtful, because nothing they built stayed around long enough to be tested.

qa.q: What could Joseph do differently with the next idea?
qa.a: Joseph could pick one idea, set a fixed stretch of time and one measure for it, and tell the team before changing course, so the test can finish.

qa.q: Why might Joseph feel each change was sensible at the time?
qa.a: After each investor chat Joseph had just heard fresh interest, so the newest idea would have looked like the safest bet.

grounding: The note shows a founder redirecting the product after each investor conversation so that nothing is tested long enough to learn from.
